name: Curse of expertise
statement: Expertise degrades judgement, and the name carries three separate claims: about novices' difficulty, about one's own understanding, and about entitlement to close-mindedness.
meaning: Three research programmes have published under this title and they do not say the same thing. Hinds asked experts to predict how long novices would need on a task, and found the prediction got worse as expertise rose. Fisher and Keil asked people to rate how well they could explain topics from their own field, and found the rating fell hardest once they tried to explain. Ottati and colleagues asked whether feeling expert makes a person closed-minded, and argued that social norms grant experts a licence to be dogmatic. The first is a claim about modelling other people, the second about modelling yourself, the third about what a role permits. Only the first shares its logic with the curse of knowledge, which is a distinct entry in this corpus and a distinct claim. Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber described a failure to subtract what you know when working out what somebody else knows. Hinds adds something that subtraction does not predict: the bias is not monotonic in knowledge, because her abstract puts intermediates ahead of experts. Earned dogmatism is not a knowledge-subtraction claim at all, and grouping it with the other two is a decision about a name rather than about a mechanism.

origin.note: The paper that attached the phrase to experts misjudging novices. Two later literatures took the same title for different claims, Fisher and Keil in 2016 for self-assessment and Ottati and colleagues from 2015 for closed-mindedness, so the year of the name and the year of each claim come apart.

evidence: Hinds's paper is paywalled, and what follows is its own abstract. In Study 1, experts, intermediate users and novices predicted how long novices would take on a complex task. Study 2 manipulated expertise instead of measuring it. Both studies found that more expertise made predictions of novice times worse, and that debiasing techniques aimed at the underestimation did not shift it. The abstract concludes that intermediates may predict novice performance more accurately than experts do. It carries no sample sizes and no effect sizes, so none are quoted here. The figures usually attached to the study, novices needing about 30 minutes against salespeople's estimate of under 13, reach this entry through a 2011 Psychology Today post by Sian Beilock and not through anything it could open. Hinds, Patterson and Pfeffer followed in 2001 with an electronic circuit-wiring task. Their abstract reports experts giving more abstract and advanced instructions and fewer concrete ones, and novices taught by beginners outperforming novices taught by experts on the target task. On a different task in the same domain the ranking reversed. Fisher and Keil tested self-assessment using the illusion-of-explanatory-depth procedure on Mechanical Turk. In Experiment 2a, 115 graduates rated how well they could explain a topic, wrote a full explanation, then rated themselves again. The drop was larger for topics inside the respondent's college major, d = 0.68, than outside it, d = 0.43. Experiment 3a, with 71 graduates, traced the gap to unnoticed forgetting since the point of peak knowledge. Ottati, Price, Wilson and Sumaktoyo ran six Mechanical Turk experiments with final samples of 34, 48, 50, 50, 28 and 50, and report all six supporting earned dogmatism. In Experiment 4 an easy trivia test lowered open-minded cognition relative to a difficult one, t(48) = 2.328, p < .03, eta-squared = .10.

replication.headline: Hinds's prediction studies have no located replication, and the one preregistered replication programme in this family split, holding for earned dogmatism's scenario manipulations and coming out at zero for its task-difficulty ones.
replication.detail: Nothing repeating Hinds was found. The 141 citing papers Semantic Scholar lists for the 1999 article contain no replication attempt, and FORRT's replication database has no row for it, for Hinds, Patterson and Pfeffer, or for Fisher and Keil. Earned dogmatism is the one strand with a record. Calin-Jageman preregistered direct replications of three of Ottati's experiments, run across a psychology participant pool and online samples in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, with materials supplied by the original team. The scenario studies held. Dogmatic behaviour was rated more appropriate for experts than for novices, d = 0.45, interval 0.35 to 0.55 pooling the replications with the original, and people imagining themselves in the expert role predicted they would be more closed-minded, d = -0.54, interval -0.64 to -0.44. The task-difficulty manipulations produced nothing: d = 0.00, interval -0.21 to 0.21 for the easy or difficult recall task, and d = -0.02, interval -0.21 to 0.17, for the easy or difficult trivia test. His preregistration puts the original trivia effect at d = 0.66, 95% interval 0.07 to 1.24, a figure he derived from Ottati's report rather than one Ottati printed. Ottati, Wilson, Osteen and Distefano replied with three further experiments they report as obtaining the effect, and read the split as evidence about manipulation quality rather than about the effect being confined to hypothetical scenarios.

study.cite: Calin-Jageman, R. J. (2018). Direct replications of Ottati et al. (2015): The earned dogmatism effect occurs only with some manipulations of expertise. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 78, 240-249.

replicated.weighting: easy versus difficult trivia manipulation, pooled across replications

limits: The strand the name came from is the strand with the least public evidence. Hinds 1999 and Hinds, Patterson and Pfeffer 2001 are both paywalled and both were read only as abstracts, which is why this entry gives neither a sample size nor an effect size for either. The 13 minutes against 30 figure sits in a Psychology Today post and is attributed there rather than to the paper. Calin-Jageman's article and Ottati's 2018 reply were also read only as abstracts. Calin-Jageman's abstract prints its intervals without naming a confidence level, and his preregistration for the same studies specifies 95%, so the intervals appear in prose here and not in the structured fields. Ottati's own samples are small and were recruited on Mechanical Turk, and his Experiment 3 reports t(76) from a study described as having 50 participants, a mismatch Calin-Jageman's preregistration also flags. Fisher and Keil's expertise is self-reported college major on Mechanical Turk, not a credential anyone checked. Searches covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar's citation list for Hinds 1999, PubMed, the Open Science Framework, FORRT's replication database at 2,624 rows, and web search.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating this as another label for the curse of knowledge. That effect is a failure to set aside what you know when judging another mind, and it predicts that bias grows with knowledge. Hinds's abstract reports intermediates predicting better than experts, which is a different shape. The second error is the cell phone numbers. They are quoted as Hinds's published result, and most readers meet them in a blog post rather than in the paper. The third is the lesson people draw from expert-taught novices doing worse. Hinds, Patterson and Pfeffer found that reversed on a different task in the same domain, so the abstract instruction that hurt on the trained task helped on transfer. The fourth is reading earned dogmatism as a finding that experts are closed-minded. It is a claim about people who feel expert in a situation, tested mostly on people asked to imagine one, and the manipulations that made participants actually succeed or fail produced nothing on replication. Fisher and Keil are also misread as showing that specialists know less than they think in general. Their measure is the drop in a self-rating after attempting an explanation, and it is largest for the topics their participants studied hardest and longest ago.
